name: principle-boundary-discipline
does: Validate external inputs once, convert them into domain types, and keep scoring and prompt construction pure behind thin adapters.
why: Boundary checks matter for generated teams and data, but you already have legality and validation contracts. Another general rule is less useful than fixing a specific missing boundary.
caveat: “Trust internal code unconditionally” is too absolute for mutable Python objects, changing legality rules and experimental pipelines. Boundary validation does not prove all later invariants.

name: principle-build-the-lever
does: Produce a small rerunnable script, generator, codemod or check for nontrivial work; verify it on one example and retain it when useful.
why: A reusable comparison or plotting script can save time across repeated experiments. The benefit depends on actual reuse; packaging a one-off task into another tool is not itself progress.
caveat: Requiring a file for every nontrivial one-off can add clutter. Use the smallest useful artifact; exploratory reasoning itself need not become a framework or script.

name: principle-encode-lessons-in-structure
does: Turn repeated corrections into enforceable types, lints, metadata, checks or scripts, and route each lesson to an actionable mechanism.
why: Encode a recurring, concrete error when a small check prevents it. Turning every correction into another rule or maintained artifact would add the kind of overhead your feedback rejects.
caveat: Not every lesson is machine-checkable. The instruction to delete textual guidance after adding enforcement can remove valuable rationale; retain judgment criteria and avoid encoding a provisional experimental choice permanently.

name: principle-exhaust-the-design-space
does: Build two or three genuinely different prototypes for novel UI or architectural choices and compare them before committing.
why: Considering a few distinct alternatives supports your interest in novel ideas and visuals. The practical benefit comes from a bounded comparison; your existing prototype and judging workflows already supply most of it.
caveat: Its bounded two-to-three option rule may simplify a bloated workflow, but applying it atop the existing variant pipeline duplicates work. “Exhaust” does not mean an exhaustive search.

name: principle-experience-first
does: Prioritize the central user workflow, polished interactions and fewer well-finished features; include maintainers and API consumers as users.
why: Your visual explanations need to help the reader understand the research. Focusing on that experience can guide useful design choices, though your existing design skills already address much of this.
caveat: Delight must serve faithful scientific explanation; feature reduction must not omit uncertainty, legality or experimental controls. This is a broad preference, not an additional implementation workflow.

name: principle-fix-root-causes
does: Reproduce and instrument failures, trace causes, repair the recurring pattern and investigate stale state when restart behavior differs.
why: Your DiBO diagnosis shows a real need to understand underlying faults. The existing diagnosing-bugs workflow already addresses this; another principle alone adds little.
caveat: “Fix all instances” can expand an experiment or cleanup beyond scope. A safeguard can be valid defense, and inability to reproduce locally does not rule out a real defect.

name: principle-foundational-thinking
does: Choose data structures and access patterns first, isolate shared mutable state, and sequence broadly useful scaffold before dependent features.
why: Questioning a weak assumption can help when a research approach stalls. Use it to choose a concrete experiment, not to justify broad restructuring before the narrow comparison you requested.
caveat: Scaffold-first and subtraction-first are heuristics. Removing baseline code or adding broad infrastructure before a narrow controlled experiment can undermine the requested comparison.

name: principle-guard-the-context-window
does: Keep bulk documents and verbose outputs out of the main context, summarize delegated work, read selectively and cap phase scope.
why: Context management is relevant, but you already use context-mode and have requested compaction controls. Another principle does not add a missing capability.
caveat: Delegation adds overhead and must remain authorized. “Finite and non-renewable” is an oversimplification in a system with compaction; summaries also risk losing evidence. All audited principle skills are manual-invocation skills.

name: principle-laziness-protocol
does: Prefer deletion, fewer layers and one source of truth; find the smallest maintainable change before adding abstractions or threaded signals.
why: Choosing a simpler sufficient implementation can accelerate experiments. It overlaps your existing guidance, and its arbitrary layering limits should not dictate architecture.
caveat: A three-layer cutoff is arbitrary. Small diffs are not always the simplest correct solution, and experiment baselines are not dead code just because a new implementation exists.

name: principle-make-operations-idempotent
does: Make repeat execution and recovery after partial failure converge by reconciling existing state, stale locks, sessions and scheduled work.
why: Safe restarts can save time during long-running experiments. Apply it to actual retry or duplicate-write problems, preserving seeds and provenance, rather than treating it as a universal new process.
caveat: Scientific sampling must not be accidentally frozen or results overwritten. Define experiment identity, seeds and intended rerun semantics; content equivalence alone does not establish identical provenance.

name: principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis
does: Inventory and migrate all internal callers, update contract tests and remove the obsolete API in one coordinated refactor when external compatibility is unnecessary.
why: Useful during a specific internal API migration, not a frequent standalone need shown by the sample. Scientific baselines may need to remain even after new code arrives.
caveat: Do not remove old methods that remain scientific baselines. The source explicitly excludes externally required compatibility; coordinated change must respect existing users and reproducibility.

name: principle-minimize-reader-load
does: Assess both indirection and hidden mutable state; collapse pass-through layers, shorten state lifetimes and require interfaces to hide meaningful complexity.
why: Readable code can make your pipelines easier to understand and change. Its contribution is gradual and overlaps existing design guidance; it is not a substitute for the explanations you ask for.
caveat: This is primarily code maintainability, not a prose-writing skill. One caller alone does not prove a boundary is useless; indiscriminate inlining can expose more complexity.

name: principle-model-the-domain

why: Clear concepts matter for teams, masks and evaluations. Your existing domain-modeling skill already covers this directly, so a second version offers limited additional benefit.
caveat: Do not confuse a typed representation with proof of game legality or predictive adequacy. This duplicates a named installed skill more than it closes a workflow gap.

name: principle-never-block-on-the-human
does: Proceed on inferable reversible work, show reviewable results and reserve questions for genuine ambiguity or irreversible actions.
